planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Zinfandel was hybridized by David Kirchhoff and registered in 1980, carrying large wine-colored self blooms with a chartreuse throat on scapes around 26 inches tall. It is a tetraploid, evergreen rebloomer, and its color holds unusually well in strong sun compared with many other dark daylilies. The cultivar earned the American Hemerocallis Society's James E. Marsh Award, given for the best purple or lavender daylily, in 1990. Grow in full sun in average garden soil and divide crowded clumps every three to four years to keep bloom counts high.

common_name: Graceful Eye Daylily (Lavender with Purple Halo)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Graceful Eye, registered by W.M. Spalding in 1981, bears large, lightly ruffled lavender flowers roughly 6 inches across, each marked with a darker purple halo around a green throat. It opens early in the season on scapes near 21 inches and builds into a dense, floriferous, evergreen diploid clump. The cultivar climbed through three American Hemerocallis Society honors: Honorable Mention in 1985, Award of Merit in 1988, and the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1989. Site it in full to part sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil for the strongest repeat bloom.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Hamlet, registered by Talbott in 1983, opens trumpet-shaped purple flowers with a darker blue-purple halo and a green throat on scapes around 18 inches. The fragrant diploid has dormant foliage, blooms early to midseason, and reblooms with extended daily flower life. It was recognized with the AHS Junior Citation in 1983, an Honorable Mention in 1987, and the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1988. Plant divisions in spring in full sun and average, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Violet Hour, registered by Peck in 1978, is a tetraploid purple self with a green throat on scapes about 25 inches tall. Foliage is dormant and the plant tolerates full sun to partial shade with unusually good cold hardiness for a purple daylily. It received the American Hemerocallis Society's James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1987. Grow in average, well-drained garden soil and divide every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Super Purple, registered by Dove in 1979, bears deep purple self flowers with a lime-green throat on a diploid, semi-evergreen plant with scapes around 27 inches. It opens in midseason and reblooms with extended daily flower life, also having earned an American Hemerocallis Society Award of Merit (1989) and Honorable Mention (1984) on its way to the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1986. The clump forms a tidy, floriferous mound well suited to mixed perennial borders. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, dividing every three to four years to sustain bloom count.

common_name: Royal Heritage Daylily (Violet-Plum with Chalky Eyezone)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Royal Heritage, registered by R.W. Munson, Jr. in 1978, carries large violet-plum flowers patterned with a chalky violet eyezone above a lemon-green throat, opening on tall scapes near 32 inches. The tetraploid, semi-evergreen plant blooms in midseason and reblooms through summer. It also received the American Hemerocallis Society's Honorable Mention in 1982, and the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1985. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, where its tall scapes hold up well above the foliage.

common_name: Sebastian Daylily (Vivid Purple with Lime-Green Throat)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Sebastian, registered by Williams in 1978, opens vivid purple self flowers with a lime-green throat on an evergreen plant that blooms in early midseason. It also earned an American Hemerocallis Society Award of Merit (1987) and Honorable Mention (1983) on its way to the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1983. Grow in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil and divide clumps every few years.

common_name: Crown Royal Daylily (Royal Purple with White Edge)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Crown Royal, registered by Steve Moldovan in 1976, bears royal-purple flowers edged in white around a darker purple eyezone and a yellow-green throat, opening on scapes near 28 inches. The dormant tetraploid blooms early in the season and reblooms, forming a compact clump. It was awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1982. Site it in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil for the cleanest white picotee edge.

common_name: Swirling Water Daylily (Purple with Cream Center Splash)

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall; set crowns with the root-to-foliage junction about an inch below soil level.

directions: Swirling Water, registered by K. Carpenter in 1979, opens purple flowers with a bold cream-white splash surrounding a green throat, carried on scapes about 22 inches above slender, semi-evergreen diploid foliage. It also received the American Hemerocallis Society's Junior Citation (1978) and Honorable Mention (1983) on its way to the James E. Marsh Award for best purple or lavender daylily in 1981. Plant divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil for dependable, long-season color.
